      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt0">brain</span> is the control center of your body. It controls your thoughts, memory, speech, and movement. It regulates the function of many organs. It's part of your nervous system, which also includes your spinal cord and peripheral nerves. The nervous system sends signals between your <span class="qt0">brain</span> and the rest of the body. Your nerves take in information from your senses and send it to the <span class="qt0">brain</span> to be processed. Your <span class="qt0">brain</span> and nerves also communicate to help you move and to control your body's functions.</p><p>When the <span class="qt0">brain</span> is healthy, it works quickly and automatically. But when you have a <span class="qt0">brain</span> disease, it may affect how  well you can function and do your daily activities. Some common <span class="qt0">brain</span> diseases include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Brain</span> tumors, which can press on nerves and affect <span class="qt0">brain</span> function.</li><li>Degenerative nerve diseases, which can affect many of your body's activities, such as balance, movement, talking, breathing, and heart function. Types include Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.</li><li>Encephalitis (inflammation in the <span class="qt0">brain</span>), which can lead to problems such as vision loss, weakness, and paralysis.</li><li>Genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders, which are caused by changes in genes (also called variants or mutations). These disorders can affect the development and function of the <span class="qt0">brain</span>.</li><li>Strokes, which can cause a loss of <span class="qt0">brain</span> cells and can affect your ability to think clearly.</li><li>Traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injuries (TBIs), which can affect <span class="qt0">brain</span> function. They may range from mild to severe. The effects of a TBI may be temporary or permanent.</li></ul><p>The symptoms of <span class="qt0">brain</span> diseases vary widely, depending on the specific problem. In some cases, damage is permanent. In other cases, treatments such as surgery, medicines, or therapies such as physical, occupational, and speech therapies, may cure the disease or improve the symptoms.</p><p> 
</p></content>

      <content name="title">Genetic <span class="qt0">Brain</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Disorders, Inborn Genetic</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Maple Syrup Urine Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Niemann-Pick Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Inborn genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorder is caused by a variation or a mutation in a gene.  A variation is a different form of a gene. A mutation is a change in a gene. Genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders affect the development and function of the <span class="qt0">brain</span>.</p><p>Some genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders are due to random gene mutations or mutations caused by environmental exposure, such as cigarette smoke. Other disorders are inherited, which means that a mutated gene or group of genes is passed down through a family. They can also be due to a combination of both genetic changes and other outside factors.</p><p>Some examples of genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders include:</p><ul><li>Leukodystrophies</li><li>Phenylketonuria</li><li>Tay-Sachs disease</li><li>Wilson disease</li></ul><p>Many people with genetic <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders fail to produce enough of certain proteins that influence <span class="qt0">brain</span> development and function. These <span class="qt0">brain</span> disorders can cause serious problems that affect the nervous system. Some have treatments to control symptoms.  Some are life-threatening.</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/braintumors.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Cancer</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Glioma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningioma</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A <span class="qt0">brain</span> tumor is a growth of abnormal cells in the tissues of the <span class="qt0">brain. Brain</span> tumors can be benign, with no cancer cells, or malignant, with cancer cells that grow quickly.  Some are primary <span class="qt0">brain</span> tumors, which start in the <span class="qt0">brain</span>. Others are metastatic, and they start somewhere else in the body and move to the <span class="qt0">brain</span>.</p><p><span class="qt0">Brain</span> tumors can cause many symptoms. Some of the most common are:</p><ul><li>Headaches, often in the morning </li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Changes in your ability to talk, hear, or see</li><li>Problems with balance or walking</li><li>Problems with thinking or memory </li><li>Feeling weak or sleepy</li><li>Changes in your mood or behavior</li><li>Seizures</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose <span class="qt0">brain</span> tumors by doing a neurologic exam and tests including an MRI, CT scan, and biopsy. Treatment options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack cancer cells with less harm to normal cells. Many people get a combination of treatments.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/concussion.html">
      <content name="title">Concussion</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Concussion</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Brain</span> Injury</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A concussion is a type of <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury.  It involves a short loss of normal <span class="qt0">brain</span> function. It happens when a hit to the head or body causes your head and <span class="qt0">brain</span> to move rapidly back and forth. This sudden movement can cause the <span class="qt0">brain</span> to bounce around or twist in the skull, creating chemical changes in your <span class="qt0">brain</span>. Sometimes it can also stretch and damage your <span class="qt0">brain</span> cells.</p><p>Sometimes people call a concussion a "mild" <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury. It is important to understand that while concussions may not be life-threatening, they can still be serious.</p><p>Concussions are a common type of sports injury. Other causes of concussions include blows to the head, bumping your head when you fall, being violently shaken, and car accidents.</p><p>Symptoms of a concussion may not start right away; they may start days or weeks after the injury. Symptoms may include a headache or neck pain. You may also have nausea, ringing in your ears, dizziness, or tiredness. You may feel dazed or not your normal self for several days or weeks after the injury. Consult your health care professional if any of your symptoms get worse, or if you have more serious symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Convulsions or seizures</li><li>Drowsiness or inability to wake up</li><li>A headache that gets worse and does not go away</li><li>Weakness, numbness, or decreased coordination</li><li>Repeated vomiting or nausea</li><li>Confusion</li><li>Slurred speech</li><li>Loss of consciousness</li></ul><p>To diagnose a concussion, your health care provider will do a physical exam and will ask about your injury. You will most likely have a neurological exam, which checks your vision, balance, coordination, and reflexes. Your health care provider may also evaluate your memory and thinking. In some cases, you may also have a scan of the <span class="qt0">brain</span>, such as a CT scan or an MRI. A scan can check for bleeding or inflammation in the <span class="qt0">brain</span>, as well as a skull fracture (break in the skull).</p><p>Most people recover fully after a concussion, but it can take some time. Rest is very important after a concussion because it helps the <span class="qt0">brain</span> to heal. In the very beginning, you may need to limit physical activities or activities that involve a lot of concentration, such as studying, working on the computer, or playing video games. Doing these may cause concussion symptoms (such as headache or tiredness) to come back or get worse. Then when your health care provider says that it is ok, you can start to return to your normal activities slowly.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/traumaticbraininjury.html">
      <content name="title">Traumatic <span class="qt0">Brain</span> Injury</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">TBI</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acquired <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI)?<p>Traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI) is a sudden injury that causes damage to the <span class="qt0">brain</span>. It may happen when there is a blow, bump, or jolt to the head. This is a closed head injury. A TBI can also happen when an object penetrates the skull. This is a penetrating injury.</p><p>Symptoms of a TBI can be mild, moderate, or severe. Concussions are a type of mild TBI. The effects of a concussion can sometimes be serious, but most people completely recover in time. More severe TBI can lead to serious physical and psychological symptoms, coma, and even death.</p>What causes traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI)?<p>The main causes of TBI depend on the type of head injury:</p><ul><li>Some of the common causes of a closed head injury include 
	<ul><li>Falls. This is the most common cause in adults age 65 and older.</li><li>Motor vehicle crashes. This is the most common cause in young adults.</li><li>Sports injuries</li><li>Being struck by an object</li><li>Child abuse. This is the most common cause in children under age 4.</li><li>Blast injuries due to explosions</li></ul>
</li><li>Some of the common causes of a penetrating injury include 
	<ul><li>Being hit by a bullet or shrapnel</li><li>Being hit by a weapon such as a hammer, knife, or baseball bat</li><li>A head injury that causes a bone fragment to penetrate the skull</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Some accidents such as explosions, natural disasters, or other extreme events can cause both closed and penetrating TBI in the same person.</p>Who is at risk for traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI)?<p>Certain groups are at higher risk of TBI:</p><ul><li>Men are more likely to get a TBI than women. They are also more likely to have serious TBI.</li><li>Adults aged 65 and older are at the greatest risk for being hospitalized and dying from a TBI</li></ul>What are the symptoms of traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI)?<p>The symptoms of TBI depend on the type of injury and how serious the <span class="qt0">brain</span> damage is.</p><p>The symptoms of mild TBI can include:</p><ul><li>A brief loss of consciousness in some cases. However, many people with mild TBI remain conscious after the injury.</li><li>Headache</li><li>Confusion</li><li>Lightheadedness</li><li>Dizziness</li><li>Blurred vision or tired eyes</li><li>Ringing in the ears</li><li>Bad taste in the mouth</li><li>Fatigue or lethargy</li><li>A change in sleep patterns</li><li>Behavioral or mood changes</li><li>Trouble with memory, concentration, attention, or thinking</li></ul><p>If you have a moderate or severe TBI, you may have those same symptoms. You may also have other symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>A headache that gets worse or does not go away</li><li>Repeated vomiting or nausea</li><li>Convulsions or seizures</li><li>Not being able to wake up from sleep</li><li>Larger than normal pupil (dark center) of one or both eyes. This is called dilation of the pupil.</li><li>Slurred speech</li><li>Weakness or numbness in the arms and legs</li><li>Loss of coordination</li><li>Increased confusion, restlessness, or agitation</li></ul>How is traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI) diagnosed?<p>If you have a head injury or other trauma that may have caused a TBI, you need to get medical care as soon as possible. To make a diagnosis, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms and the details of your injury</li><li>Will do a neurologic exam</li><li>May do imaging tests, such as a CT scan or MRI</li><li>May use a tool such as the Glasgow coma scale to determine how severe the TBI is. This scale measures your ability to open your eyes, speak, and move.</li><li>May do neuropsychological tests to check how your <span class="qt0">brain</span> is functioning</li></ul>What are the treatments for traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI)?<p>The treatments for TBI depend on many factors, including the size, severity, and location of the <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury.</p><p>For mild TBI, the main treatment is rest. If you have a headache, you can try taking over-the-counter pain relievers. It is important to follow your health care provider's instructions for complete rest and a gradual return to your normal activities. If you start doing too much too soon, it may take longer to recover. Contact your provider if your symptoms are not getting better or if you have new symptoms.</p><p>For moderate to severe TBI, the first thing health care providers will do is stabilize you to prevent further injury. They will manage your blood pressure, check the pressure inside your skull, and make sure that there is enough blood and oxygen getting to your <span class="qt0">brain</span>.</p><p>Once you are stable, the treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery to reduce additional damage to your <span class="qt0">brain</span>, for example to
	<ul><li>Remove hematomas (clotted blood)</li><li>Get rid of damaged or dead <span class="qt0">brain</span> tissue</li><li>Repair skull fractures</li><li>Relieve pressure in the skull</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines to treat the symptoms of TBI and to lower some of the risks associated with it, such as
	<ul><li>Anti-anxiety medication to lessen feelings of nervousness and fear</li><li>Anticoagulants to prevent blood clots</li><li>Anticonvulsants to prevent seizures</li><li>Antidepressants to treat symptoms of depression and mood instability</li><li>Muscle relaxants to reduce muscle spasms</li><li>Stimulants to increase alertness and attention</li></ul>
</li><li>Rehabilitation therapies, which can include therapies for physical, emotional, and cognitive difficulties:
	<ul><li>Physical therapy, to build physical strength, coordination, and flexibility</li><li>Occupational therapy, to help you learn or relearn how to perform daily tasks, such as getting dressed, cooking, and bathing</li><li>Speech therapy, to help you to with speech and other communication skills and treat swallowing disorders</li><li>Psychological counseling, to help you learn coping skills, work on relationships, and improve your emotional well-being</li><li>Vocational counseling, which focuses on your ability to return to work and deal with workplace challenges</li><li>Cognitive therapy, to improve your memory, attention, perception, learning, planning, and judgment</li></ul></li></ul><p>Some people with TBI may have permanent disabilities. A TBI can also put you at risk for other health problems such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Treating these problems can improve your quality of life.</p>Can traumatic <span class="qt0">brain</span> injury (TBI) be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to prevent head injuries and TBIs:</p><ul><li>Always wear your seatbelt and use car seats and booster seats for children</li><li>Never drive under the influence of drugs or alcohol</li><li>Wear a properly fitting helmet when riding a bicycle, skateboarding, and playing sports like hockey and football</li><li>Prevent falls by
	<ul><li>Making your house safer. For example, you can install railings on the stairs and grab bars in the tub, get rid of tripping hazards, and use window guards and stair safety gates for young children.</li><li>Improving your balance and strength with regular physical activity</li></ul>
</li></ul></content>
